verdict.rationale: GrowthBook's docs say metrics are built mainly on Fact Tables, where users write SQL against their own warehouse (11 sources including BigQuery, Snowflake and Databricks) and define multiple metrics on top. Independent users confirm it runs on existing click-stream data through views and supports any metric expressible as a query, unlike walled-garden event stores. The 'coupling metrics' critique is an opinion, not a counter-example. missing for 10: documented detail on an ingested-events (non-warehouse) metric path, and specifics of the supported metric types and definitions.

support.subject: As a product manager, I can define experiment metrics from my own data — warehouse tables or ingested events — instead of a black-box metric store

citations.quote: The primary way to create metrics in GrowthBook is with Fact Tables where you write SQL to pull a set of rows and then define multiple metrics on top of those rows.
Define Fact Tables and metrics so GrowthBook can compute experiment results from your warehouse.
Warehouse Native. Query 11 data sources including BigQuery, Snowflake, and Databricks.
GrowthBook (like Eppo) connects to your existing data warehouse and supports any metric you can express as a query.
Optimizely is a walled garden, you need to push all your metrics as events; Eppo and GrowthBook both connect to your data warehouse instead.
